cases.description: A complete card-fetch, version-select, signed request, and accepted response verifies.
When both sides support ink/0.2, the higher preferred common version is selected and pinned.
A non-200 discovery response fails the fetch step and rejects the transcript.
A card whose agentId does not equal the requested agentId fails the identity binding.
When the card and client share no protocol version, selection fails and the transcript rejects.
A request emitted under a version the card does not advertise rejects.
A tampered request signature fails verification.
A request payload missing the required context fails the connection_request schema.
A request envelope whose intent is not connection_request rejects.
A transport timestamp that disagrees with the request envelope timestamp rejects (§3.3 binding).
A request nonce already in the receiver's seen set is a replay and rejects.
A request older than the freshness window against the receiver clock rejects.
A tampered response signature fails verification.
A connection_response whose status is not accepted rejects the first-contact transcript.
A connection_response payload with an unknown key fails the strict schema.
A response emitted under a different version than the selected one rejects.
A response envelope whose intent is not connection_response rejects.
A transport timestamp that disagrees with the response envelope timestamp rejects (§3.3 binding).
A request timestamp beyond the future skew against the receiver clock rejects.
A card without supportedProtocolVersions defaults to ink/0.1 and the ink/0.1 flow accepts.
A card advertising an empty version list defaults to ink/0.1 and accepts.

A receiver that advertises a different inbound path accepts a request signed over that path. INK reserves no fixed inbound path: PATH is the path component of the card's endpoint, so an implementation that hardcodes one spelling rejects a conforming peer.

A request whose signed path is not the path component of the fetched card's endpoint rejects, even though the signature over that path is itself valid. PATH is inside the frozen signature base, so a sender that signs a path from a document instead of from the card it just fetched cannot be verified by the receiver at its real endpoint.

A request envelope with no `id` rejects. §3.1 makes id, correlationId, createdAt and signature MUSTs, so a receiver validates the envelope before it verifies anything; here both signatures verify over the shortened envelope, so the structure step is the only thing that can reject it.
The same §3.1 obligation on the response half: an envelope with no `createdAt` rejects even though the response is otherwise a correctly signed accepted connection_response.

The intent envelope is a strict surface (§3.1, compatibility-policy §3.1): an unknown top-level member rejects. The member is present before signing, so both signatures cover it and only the strict schema can reject.

A request envelope whose §3.6 body signature was made with the receiver's key rather than the sender's rejects. The transport signature is valid over the delivered body, so an implementation that verifies only the §3.3 transport signature and treats the envelope `signature` member as opaque accepts a body the named sender never signed.
The same on the response half: the receiver's envelope carries a body signature made with the sender's key, and the sender must reject it.
